# Reproducing the Laboratory Package {#sec-reproducible-labs}

For the guided ASIC activities, read @sec-vlsi-design before interpreting technology results and @sec-physical-validation for scan, memory-test and release-review exercises. The scan teaching model can be simulated separately; technology scan insertion, fault coverage and physical validation require the additional tools and collateral identified there.

This appendix turns the book's small examples into a repeatable laboratory workflow. The package contains complete reference RTL, independent checks, assembly, driver code, flow inputs and guides. It also identifies activities that need a board, a physical-design environment or a student implementation.

**A physical FPGA is optional for the online course.** The [alternative guide](../labs/NO-FPGA.md), also included in the downloadable ZIP, reviews all eighteen labs and specifies replacements for physical programming and observations. Use RTL simulation for functional behavior and real-Wally firmware execution, plus synthesis/constraint analysis and generated or instructor-provided implementation reports for P5. The board route remains available. Both routes use the coursework rubric in @sec-hsd-coursework; unexecuted board checks remain explicit qualification gaps.

For the 12-week Hardware System Design course, @sec-hsd-coursework maps reference activities to assessed practices, autonomous work, deliverables and rubrics. It defines an AXI/DMA accelerator controlled by Wally as the project backbone. The executable reference in @sec-executable-project supplies the AXI/DMA IP, bounded formal checks and Wally firmware platform. The Wally clone is an explicit external dependency.

[Download the laboratory package](../downloads/hardware-design-labs.zip). The executable files are versioned under `labs/` and `examples/` in the book repository. Extract the ZIP and run commands from its root, where `labs/run.py` is located. Its quick-start README and lab guides accompany the code, tests, firmware, flow inputs and licenses. The book's chapters, appendices, illustrations and bibliography are excluded; read HTML or download the complete PDF separately. `LAB-PROVENANCE.json` records the chapter origins, listing selectors and chapter/code fingerprints without copying the chapter text.

Alternatively, obtain the repository:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/antoniofloresgil/FromConceptToSiliconBook.git
cd FromConceptToSiliconBook
```

## Select an activity and its verification boundary

### Recipe status, shell and working directory

| Status | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Checked recipe** | Executed with recorded tools/inputs and stated scope | Automatic labs; real Wally accelerator/divider runs; older Sail signature test |
| **Adaptation template** | Review external versions, paths, technology or API options first | Physical Tcl, board programming, modern Sail command, gem5 sketch |
| **Exercise** | Implement/extend a design or check and produce new evidence | New accelerator features and full-SoC scenarios |

: Recipe status values, their meaning and examples {#tbl-reproducible-labs-recipe-status-values-meaning}

Source export, synthesis, tool discovery and full physical qualification are different boundaries. A block inherits its section's stated scope, not an automatic claim of execution.

Start at the repository/extracted-package root unless stated otherwise. `cd` changes the directory for subsequent commands. Bash/WSL uses `\` for continuation; PowerShell uses a backtick. Prompts, output listings and angle-bracket placeholders are not shell commands. Paths and HDL ports are case-sensitive on Linux.

| Entry point | Scope | Automatic evidence |
|---|---|---|
| `foundations` | ISA fields, decoder, ALU, register file, iterative arithmetic and basic RTL | Vector comparisons, state/latency and reset tests |
| `memory` | Synchronous memory and functional cache model | Byte masks, read-first, stalls, dirty-data preservation |
| `transport` | Queues and request/response paths | Ordering, capacity, retained payloads and reset effects |
| `mmio` | AXI-Lite/APB, FIFO, PWM and UART/SPI driver source | Transaction tests and freestanding driver compilation |
| `verilator` | Existing accumulator with C++ testbench | Scoreboard and VCD |
| `cocotb` | Same accumulator with Python testbench | Scoreboard and XML test report |
| `isa` | RV32I demonstration and linker layout | ELF/signature check in a small program-specific oracle |
| `synthesis` | All complete teaching units and implementation accumulator | Behavioral test, elaboration, no unintended latches, generic netlist |
| `fpga`, `asic`, `wally` | Board, PDK or full-system integration | Guided work with separately collected evidence |
| `accelerator` | FIR/extension design task | Student implementation and test plan |
| `dotproduct` | Complete AXI/DMA signed dot-product IP | All lengths, errors/security/reuse, synthesis and bounded properties |
| `dotproduct-wally` | Real Wally, AHB adapter and firmware | Explicit external entry: polling, interrupt handler and result/cycle checks |
| `mmu` | Sv32 aliases, S-mode and a delegated store page fault | Separate Spike test with expected signature; guided Wally trace |
| `dse` | Controlled actual Wally divider sweep and illustrative Pareto analysis | Checked explicit script with external clone; outside `run all` |

: Entry points, their scope and automatic evidence {#tbl-reproducible-labs-entry-points-scope-automatic}

`run all` executes the nine automatic entries. A missing board, PDK or unfinished accelerator is never counted as a pass. An automatic result covers the tested boundary, and the other requirements of the subsystem need their own checks.

The optional [hardware-generators practice](../labs/19-hardware-generators/README.md), introduced in @sec-hardware-generators, compares a Chisel accumulator with direct SystemVerilog through an independent scoreboard and a deliberately faulty generator. Its separate image supplies Scala/Chisel and CIRCT; it requires no FPGA and remains outside the nine automatic entries. The compact reference preserves generated RTL, intermediate representations and separately scoped generic synthesis statistics.

The advanced [multicore practice](../labs/20-multicore/README.md) in @sec-multicore executes Linux on two QEMU CPUs with the existing DMA driver/model. It checks pinned-CPU publication, 64 handoffs and 32 contending jobs. Separate finite cache/visibility/dependency models expose stale-data and progress mistakes; they stop short of coherent Wally RTL and physical performance evidence. This practice is outside the nine automatic entries and the compulsory twelve-week workload.

The optional [physical-closure continuation](../labs/21-physical-closure/README.md) in @sec-complete-closure preserves the complete-case baseline and executes lower-clock, registered-product and physical-repair candidates. It supplies fresh routed FPGA results, extracted ASIC setup/hold/electrical reports, functional mapped/routed equivalence and actual geometry captures. Its qualified result is restricted to the declared single-corner block gate; manufacturing DRC/LVS and full-SoC/board acceptance remain open. It requires no physical FPGA and remains outside `run all` and the compulsory workload.

The optional [layout-verification continuation](../labs/22-layout-verification/README.md) in @sec-layout-verification executes actual GDS DRC and transistor-level LVS with the available FreePDK45 reference technology. It diagnoses missing power/body connectivity, finishes a separate layout, re-extracts timing and rejects deliberately faulty geometry. Passing public-reference checks is distinct from foundry manufacturing qualification. The compact dossier is auditable without EDA tools; actual reproduction uses the same pinned ORFS image and remains outside `run all`.

The `mmu` guide uses the complete files in `examples/privileged-mmu/` and the commands in @sec-privileged-mmu. Its architectural test was checked with GCC 13.2.0 and Spike 1.1.1-dev; the reference suite also rejects a variant that makes the intentionally read-only alias writable. Spike and the cross toolchain are separate dependencies. This activity sits outside the small container's nine automatic labs, and its Spike pass does not claim a Wally RTL execution.

## The supplied simulation and synthesis container

The package provides `labs/Dockerfile`. Build it locally as `from-concept-labs:2026.10`; this name is a local tag, not a published image that students should expect to pull.

The image supplies Python, Icarus, standalone Verilator, Yosys, Clang/LLD, Make, a C++ compiler and cocotb 2.0.1. Ubuntu 24.04 is pinned by its base-image digest. Distribution package versions are resolved when building and recorded by the runner; preserve a built image for a cohort if exact environment reuse is required.

The tested Linux x86-64 baseline passed all nine automatic entries with Python 3.12.3, Icarus 12.0, Verilator 5.020, Yosys 0.33 and cocotb 2.0.1. `labs/validated-environment.json` in the package records its image ID and full tool versions. The deliberate FIFO-loss test also confirms that a design defect produces a failing simulation; it is an expected negative test, kept separate from the passing reference report.

With Docker installed and its Linux-container engine running, use these commands from the repository/package root:

```bash
docker build -f labs/Dockerfile -t from-concept-labs:2026.10 .
docker run --rm --network none --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" --env HOME=/tmp \
  --mount "type=bind,source=$PWD,target=/work" \
  from-concept-labs:2026.10
```

The preceding **checked Linux/WSL runtime recipe** uses the host UID/GID for writable mounts, matching Actions, and a writable `HOME=/tmp` [@reproductionDockerRun]. Dependency installation belongs to image building, not offline execution. The PowerShell recipe below targets Docker Desktop and a Windows checkout with Windows access controls. For a Linux/WSL checkout, use the Linux recipe; POSIX `id` expressions are not a PowerShell UID mapping. PowerShell uses its own interpolation syntax:

```powershell
docker build -f labs/Dockerfile -t from-concept-labs:2026.10 .
docker run --rm --network none --env HOME=/tmp `
  --mount "type=bind,source=${PWD},target=/work" `
  from-concept-labs:2026.10
```

The build downloads dependencies. The automatic execution uses `--network none`, mounts only the project directory and writes results under `labs/build/`. It does not mount the Docker socket or acquire board USB permissions. `--rm` removes the execution container, while the locally built image remains available for the next practice.

To inspect the environment or run one practice, override its default command:

```bash
docker run --rm --network none --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" --env HOME=/tmp --mount "type=bind,source=$PWD,target=/work" \
  from-concept-labs:2026.10 python labs/run.py doctor
docker run --rm --network none --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" --env HOME=/tmp --mount "type=bind,source=$PWD,target=/work" \
  from-concept-labs:2026.10 python labs/run.py run transport --seed 2027
```

Use the PowerShell mount form above on Windows. Python-only `list`, `check` and `pack` also run on a native Windows Python installation. Linux hardware tools can run in this container or an appropriately configured WSL environment.

The cocotb baseline explicitly chooses Icarus. cocotb 2.0.1 supports Icarus 11.0 or later, while its Verilator backend needs 5.036 or later; the standalone C++ Verilator example has a different compatibility boundary [@cocotbLabSupport]. A working standalone Verilator installation may not be able to host this cocotb version.

## Native Linux execution

### Existing Linux build files owned by root

The new `--user` options prevent new root-owned files but do not repair old output. From the project root, inspect the specific build directory. If it contains results from an earlier root container, repair only that directory:

```bash
ls -ld labs/build
sudo chown -R --no-dereference "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -- labs/build
```

This is a **conditional repair**, requiring permission to change ownership and this project's existing `labs/build/`. Limit the repair to that directory, since a whole repository or a system directory is far too broad. Rerun the corrected recipe and check that the host user can append to a generated result. Global permissive modes are unnecessary.

### Native installation template

**Adaptation template:** distribution packages depend on the repository date. Record actual versions after installation. The runner needs Python 3.10+, even though the standalone cocotb test has a lower Python minimum.

The container is the shared coursework baseline. Native installations can use the same Python entry point if all required programs are on PATH. On Ubuntu 24.04, install the simulation/synthesis dependencies and a virtual environment:

```bash
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install python3-venv python3-dev iverilog verilator yosys clang lld make g++ git
python3 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r labs/requirements.txt
python labs/run.py doctor
python labs/run.py run all
```

The Python development package supplies the shared library cocotb embeds. If `find_libpython` cannot find that library, fix the installation before running the simulator. The native package versions need not match an earlier container build. Include the resulting environment report in comparisons. An unrelated local development image is not evidence of a reproducible student environment unless its recipe and identity are also available.

## Sources, seeds and result records

### Shared interfaces and versions

| Material | Exact interface/source | Checked boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C++/cocotb accumulator | `examples/verilator/accumulator.sv`: `clk`, `reset`, `Clear`, `Enable`, `Operand`, `Sum`, `Valid`, `Overflow` | One-operand simulation; C++ and Python tests |
| Physical-flow accumulator | `labs/07-implementation/rtl/accumulator.sv`: `Clk`, `Reset`, `Clear`, `Enable`, `A`, `B`, `Sum`, `Valid`, `Overflow` | Dedicated unit test/generic synthesis; physical flow requires technology inputs |
| Laboratory runner | Python 3.10+, `labs/run.py`, repository/package root | Native Python-only commands; hardware runs with the stated tools |
| cocotb standalone test | cocotb 2.0.1, Python 3.9+, Icarus 11+; checked Icarus 12.0 | Its Makefile defaults to Icarus and shared one-operand RTL |
| Standalone Verilator | Checked 5.020 for C++ and Wally fixtures | Does not meet cocotb 2.0.1's separate Verilator-backend minimum |

: Shared interfaces, exact versions and the checked boundary {#tbl-reproducible-labs-shared-interfaces-exact-versions}

Both designs use the top name `accumulator`, but their ports and operand contracts differ. The physical YAML/SDC uses `Clk` and references the implementation RTL. Running the earlier cocotb test only checks its own source. See `labs/recipe-contracts.json` and run `python labs/tools/check_recipes.py` for static case/path/port/version checks. It also checks Linux Docker flags and Wally's report namespace; it does not execute external tools or validate a new technology.

Local unit runs write `labs/build/report.json`. The Wally recipe sets `LAB_BUILD_DIR=/work/labs/build/wally-platform` so the system report is `labs/build/wally-platform/report.json`; native Linux sets the equivalent path `labs/build/wally-platform`. Preserve both for the evidence collector. DSE writes `labs/build/dse/results.json` locally; CI uses its separate `dse-platform/` namespace.

In the full repository, the runner checks that exported reference files match their chapter listings before simulation and packaging. `labs/tools/catalog.py` records the source chapter, language and listing selector; the existing Verilator/cocotb examples are checked too. In an extracted practice ZIP, the runner instead checks package integrity and listing identities against `LAB-PROVENANCE.json`. Chapter/code equality was checked when the archive was produced. The manifest identifies the originating source revision and any tracked local preview edits; its hashes detect accidental drift rather than signing the archive. Authoring commands `sync` and `pack` require the full repository.

```bash
python labs/run.py check
python labs/run.py list
python labs/run.py run memory --seed 2026
```

Authors use `sync` after reviewing an intentional chapter edit. That command regenerates exported reference files. Students should keep variants separately:

```bash
mkdir -p labs/work/transport
cp -r labs/03-transport/rtl labs/work/transport/rtl
python labs/run.py run transport --rtl-dir labs/work/transport/rtl --seed 2026
```

Copy the complete RTL directory, preserving module names and dependencies. On Windows, use `New-Item` and `Copy-Item` or the editor to make the same directory. The variant's hashes appear in the result record, while the reference material remains unchanged.

`labs/build/report.json` records source hashes, actual per-lab seed, environment, commands, exit codes, logs and artifact hashes. The original Verilator/cocotb stimuli retain fixed seed 2026. New randomized tests use the selected seed. Compile failure, timeout, a failing assertion, missing dependency or an empty/failed cocotb suite produces a failing command and nonzero overall exit code.

A minimized waveform and an explained requirement should accompany a failure report. A repaired design needs a new passing run and a retained regression case. CI executes the automatic suite on pushes and pull requests and preserves logs and reports as an artifact; board programming and ASIC signoff stay outside it.

## Cold-environment reproduction audits {#sec-cold-reproduction-audit}

Checking retained reports confirms their internal integrity, and reproducing a result means executing its tools again. The repository's [cold-audit protocol](https://github.com/antoniofloresgil/FromConceptToSiliconBook/blob/main/tools/reproducibility/README.md) starts from a fresh public clone and rebuilds the documented environments, then selects formal, Linux/QEMU, FPGA and ASIC experiments. It requires read-only source/reference protection, fresh outputs, recorded image identities, artifact hashes and deliberate rejection tests. A physical runner's `completed` status must still be distinguished from passing its timing or layout acceptance criteria.

The [19 October 2026 audit record](https://github.com/antoniofloresgil/FromConceptToSiliconBook/blob/main/docs/audits/2026-10-19/README.md) identifies the audited revision, execution evidence and limits of an agent-executed clean-container review. An independent human review, board validation and foundry qualification remain separate steps. The accompanying integrity helper checks source snapshots and raw report hashes without invoking EDA tools; it cannot substitute for rerunning a laboratory.

## Continuous hardware verification of the accelerator {#sec-hardware-ci}

[Core · P5 · C1](../learning-paths.qmd#sec-path-labels){#act-hardware-ci .learning-activity}

Reproducible tools become useful regression infrastructure when a change produces a decision tied to the affected hardware. [Lab 25](../labs/25-hardware-ci/README.md) runs the existing AXI/DMA accelerator through one chain, using the same snapshotted RTL throughout:

```text
Lint -> Elaboration -> Simulation -> Formal -> Synthesis -> Reports
```

This is an executable application of the plan in @sec-verification-methodology. It adds no new hardware feature. The RTL remains the Lab 10 baseline; candidates are copied into a separate directory. The stages share source hashes, seed 2026, configuration, tool versions and one result record. A failed stage stops dependent work. Later stages are `skipped`, not successful by absence.

### What each stage must establish

| Stage | Executed check | Rejection condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lint | Verilator checks the actual accelerator hierarchy | Tool mismatch, syntax/error diagnostic or unreviewed warning |
| Elaboration | Yosys resolves hierarchy/processes and exports the interface | Missing module, structural inconsistency, changed port/default-parameter contract |
| Simulation | Independent Lab 10 scoreboard at maximum lengths 256 and 16; AHB bridge test | Arithmetic, ordering, strobe, DMA-window, error, completion, interrupt/reset or stall assertion failure |
| Formal | Existing bounded RTL assertions plus reachable completion witness | Failed assertion, timeout or missing successful proof/witness |
| Synthesis | Flattened generic mapping of the default 256-element-capacity configuration | Structural error, unintended latch or failed synthesis |
| Reports | Compare mapped cell count with the reviewed budget; recheck source identity | Excessive logic growth or changed inputs |

: Stages of the hardware CI, the check each executes and its rejection condition {#tbl-reproducible-labs-stages-hardware-ci-check}

The elaborated [contract](../labs/25-hardware-ci/contract.json) records port names, directions, widths, signedness and default parameters. It catches a changed interface even if a testbench happens not to exercise the affected bits. It does not encode every AXI or register semantic rule. Independent transactions and assertions check those behaviors. An intended ABI change needs explicit integration/test review, not an edit that makes the old checker agree automatically.

Lint also needs an explicit policy. The preserved RTL produces six reviewed diagnostics: four implicit unsigned address extensions in 33-bit range comparisons, the unused engine-busy indication, and the unused upper half of a 32-bit DMA operand. The runner uses `-Wno-fatal` to collect diagnostics, then compares the **exact reviewed multiset** of warning codes, source filenames and messages. Additional, changed or missing messages fail. It does not globally accept a warning category. Logs retain all six observations, and an intentional cleanup requires updating the reviewed expectation.

The formal stage retains its original boundary: 20-cycle symbolic control BMC and a 24-cycle engine check with a fixed valid length-one descriptor and a reachable DONE witness. The witness helps expose a vacuous completion argument. Induction, unrestricted AXI compliance, full arithmetic correctness and unbounded progress remain outside these checks. The standalone FIFO chapter in @sec-formal-verification develops those proof distinctions more fully.

### A metric gate needs a stable denominator

The actual reference produces **5,662 generic cells** with Yosys 0.33, after flattening the same top and mapping with the same recipe. The [policy](../labs/25-hardware-ci/policy.json) sets:

$$N_{\mathrm{limit}} = \left\lceil 1.05\times 5662\right\rceil = 5946.$$

Five percent is a declared teaching **review budget** for logical growth. It allows small deliberate changes within the fixed configuration while flagging a larger increase for an engineering decision. It is not a technology limit or a claim that every 4% increase is acceptable. Tool versions are checked before running the gate; changing the mapper can change the cell denominator without changing the RTL.

Generic cells are not square micrometres, watts or nanoseconds. The gate cannot reject a timing regression that only appears after routing. A product could instead budget a characterized cell area, extracted slack or workload latency, but each requires its own configuration and measurement contract. Keep such a decision separate from this fast count comparison.

The runner never learns a new baseline from the current candidate. For an intended architecture change, inspect the failing report, explain the cost and functional consequences, rerun relevant system/physical checks, and review a new policy explicitly. Repository review and branch-protection settings remain administrative controls; adding a workflow file does not configure them.

### Demonstrate that rejection actually works

The [recorded dossier](../labs/25-hardware-ci/reference/negative-results.json) contains four real modified copies of the RTL, passed through the same entry point:

| Modification | First failing stage | Observed evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Change default `MAX_LENGTH` from 256 to 257 | Elaboration | Elaborated parameter contract mismatch |
| Make multiplication unsigned | Simulation | Independent arithmetic mismatch |
| Insert a deliberately false formal assertion | Formal | Failed bounded assertion and VCD counterexample |
| Add a retained unused 256-bit counter | Reports | **6,668 cells**, exceeding the **5,946** limit |

: Modifications that must be rejected, the first failing stage and the evidence {#tbl-reproducible-labs-modifications-must-be-rejected}

The last candidate passes lint, elaboration, simulation, bounded formal checks and synthesis. Its counter is deliberately retained so optimization cannot remove the experiment. It demonstrates a cost regression that functional tests alone would accept. The false assertion is a sensitivity test for the formal stage, not a previously hidden defect in the healthy accelerator. The [positive run](../labs/25-hardware-ci/reference/positive/report.json) passes all six stages at 5,662 cells.

Reproduce the positive run with the ordinary lab image using the Linux/WSL or PowerShell commands in the guide. Sources are mounted read-only; a separate writable mount receives results. Run `negative.py` in the same environment to challenge all four gates. Alternatively, `verify_reference.py` audits the delivered transcripts, source/artifact hashes, actual generic netlists and failure outcomes using Python only. Auditing recorded evidence is not rerunning EDA tools.

### Separate per-change checks from physical campaigns

The publication workflow calls the dedicated [accelerator workflow](../labs/25-hardware-ci/reference/workflows/hardware-ci.yml) on main-branch pushes and pull requests, alongside the broader laboratory/Wally regression. The book build requires both jobs. The accelerator job executes the healthy chain and negative controls offline after image construction, and uploads its evidence even on failure. Preserve the first diagnostic, failed-stage identity and counterexample rather than presenting only the final red status.

| Tier | Trigger and scope | Evidence and limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Per change | Main push / pull request; lint through generic synthesis | Interface, independent tests, bounded proof/witness, cell budget; no routed timing |
| Wider functional campaign | Existing laboratory/Wally jobs; explicit additional configurations | Broader software/system evidence; no inherited whole-core proof |
| Physical implementation | Explicit dispatch of the separate physical workflow; other FPGA/ASIC sweeps through Labs 21–22 | Fresh routing/extraction and target-specific acceptance; longer runtime and additional images/PDK |

: Workflow tiers, their trigger and scope, and the evidence limit {#tbl-reproducible-labs-workflow-tiers-trigger-scope}

The new manual [ASIC workflow](../labs/25-hardware-ci/reference/workflows/physical-regression.yml) first requires a fresh fast gate at the same Git revision. It then uses the pinned ORFS image to implement the Lab 21 repaired 100 MHz block and check mapped/routed equivalence. `physical_gate.py` requires nonnegative extracted setup and hold, zero reported electrical violations, no unconstrained-path report, an empty final router DRC report and valid nonempty GDS readback. Its scope is Nangate45 typical with the block's supplied interface budgets. Reference-PDK transistor LVS and geometry DRC retain their separate Lab 22 campaign; manufacturing qualification remains open.

The physical runner also enforces the locked Lab 17 RTL manifest. Changing the accelerator cannot silently reuse the historical physical result. A new implementation candidate needs an explicitly reviewed manifest/configuration and fresh physical runs, following @sec-complete-closure. FPGA sweeps remain separate reproducible commands, not an implied side effect of this ASIC job.

The healthy chain and all four mutations were executed locally in Docker with network disabled, UID/GID 1000 and read-only sources. The physical acceptance helper was checked against the existing actual repaired-block run, retaining setup **+5.20410 ns** and hold **+0.02968 ns**. This addition supplies workflow definitions and locally executed evidence; it does not claim a new physical campaign or an observed GitHub-hosted Actions execution.

For assessment, submit one passing candidate, one minimized rejection and its first failing stage. Explain why the 6,668-cell candidate can be functionally correct yet rejected, which configuration makes the comparison meaningful, and what new evidence would justify replacing the baseline. Then identify a possible routed-timing regression that this fast chain cannot detect.

## Preserve and share an environment

Record both the package checksum and built-image identity:

```bash
python labs/run.py pack
docker image inspect from-concept-labs:2026.10 --format '{{.Id}}'
docker save -o labs/build/from-concept-labs.tar from-concept-labs:2026.10
```

Create `labs/build/` first if no run has created it. Another machine can use `docker load -i labs/build/from-concept-labs.tar`. The TAR is a large build artifact and stays outside version control. Running the same saved image removes dependency resolution from later practical sessions; rebuilding a mutable package repository can produce another image even with the same local tag.

The ZIP contains `SHA256SUMS.json`; `check` also verifies those checksums when running an extracted package, and `pack` prints the ZIP's SHA-256. Packaging excludes reports, virtual environments, caches, simulator output and student work. Quarto's pre-render step generates the ZIP and publishes it as a book resource; it does not execute hardware tests while rendering.

: External repositories and environments and how each is used {#tbl-reproducible-labs-external-repositories-environments-used}

For the Wally baseline inspected in this book:

```bash
git clone --branch opensource-fpga-bitstream https://github.com/antoniofloresgil/cvw.git
cd cvw
git checkout 3b30ba6b6519bd2c26c1437e6d61f632a35cef6c
git submodule update --init --recursive
git rev-parse HEAD
```

Obtain toolchains, chip databases and board support using that revision's instructions and the FPGA chapters. The small container includes the Clang/LLD and ELF-loading helpers used by its checked virtual-platform recipes; it does not include the complete Wally board/cross toolchain, nextpnr-Xilinx databases, DDR controller environment or a physical board firmware loader. Keep the build script, selected parameters, images and constraint files alongside the revision.

Use on-chip-memory firmware for the first board milestone. At the documented branch snapshot, DDR3 service initialization is an additional unresolved bring-up activity. A generated bitstream does not show that every external-memory path works.

**Adaptation template (checked tool discovery only):** for ASIC work, use the separately installed ORFS environment [@orfsLabContainers]. A local `openroad/orfs:latest` was inspected while preparing the package. Its `/OpenROAD-flow-scripts/env.sh` puts the installed OpenROAD and Yosys binaries on PATH. A checked tool-discovery command is:

```bash
docker run --rm --network none --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" --env HOME=/tmp openroad/orfs:latest \
  bash -lc 'source /OpenROAD-flow-scripts/env.sh; openroad -version'
docker image inspect openroad/orfs:latest --format '{{json .RepoDigests}}'
```

Obtain the image separately if it is not installed. `latest` is not a reproducibility identifier: record its digest and the ORFS/platform revisions. The inspected image digest was `fd3e27cf1788815be526e86fbe449310d1114bf256fd6c7af9dced6eaf12c699`; it identifies that image, not a tested hardening result. Follow the OpenROAD chapter for direct Tcl and ORFS variants with the appropriate platform inputs.

**Adaptation template:** LibreLane documents a Nix-based setup and its supported operating environments [@librelaneLabSetup]. This is a separate environment from the supplied lab Docker image. In that environment, use `labs/07-implementation/config.yaml`, whose `VERILOG_FILES` resolves to the accompanying uppercase-`Clk` implementation RTL. Supply the chosen PDK root and preserve the resolved flow configuration.

LibreLane also documents a Dockerized CLI setup [@librelaneLabDocker]. After installing a selected LibreLane version in its own Python environment and configuring Docker, its documented smoke-test command is:

```bash
python -m librelane --dockerized --smoke-test
```

Then run the laboratory configuration with the selected PDK root:

```bash
cd labs/07-implementation
python -m librelane --dockerized --pdk-root "$PDK_ROOT" config.yaml
```

This command belongs to the guided ASIC activity and has additional image/PDK downloads and physical checks. Record the CLI version and tool-image identity; the automatic suite does not claim to have completed that flow.

For both ASIC options, report corners, clock/IO constraints, PDK/SCL identity, setup/hold results, physical-check results and final file provenance. For FPGA with a board, report the board/device, pin constraints, timing/resources, programming result and software-visible milestone. Without a board, use [Lab 07's alternative](../labs/07-implementation/README.md#without-a-physical-board): archive generated or provided implementation reports, explain constraints and timing, execute the real-Wally functional milestone and submit expected bring-up checkpoints. Mark programming and physical observations as unexecuted. FPGA tools/databases are still needed to build a `.bit`, but a connected board is needed only for programming and observation. These guided checks complement the automatic unit suite.

Run/boot status, source hashes and parameters remain separate from the bare-metal and physical profiles. The guide supplies Linux/WSL and PowerShell commands for the full period/utilization campaign, actual GUI exports and hash-checked summaries. @sec-openroad-study analyses eight routed and three rejected cases, including a positive post-CTS setup margin that becomes negative after routing/extraction. Reports accompany the ZIP; book figures are read online or regenerated. `python labs/16-openroad-study/verify_reference.py` checks the preserved report/source identities without executing physical tools. The standalone [formal FIFO practice](../labs/15-formal/README.md) supports @sec-formal-verification using the existing teaching image. Run `python labs/15-formal/run.py` as its container command; its guide gives Linux/WSL and PowerShell recipes. It records BMC, induction/equivalence, reachability/vacuity controls, the defect counterexample and repaired/faulty simulation regression under `labs/build/formal/`. It runs explicitly outside the nine automatic entries and is checked separately by CI. Its FIFO equivalence proof does not close `DP-EQUIV` for the accelerator.

Use @sec-verification-methodology for the requirement-driven hierarchy from RTL to physical release and production test. The package includes `labs/verification/project-plan.json`, a reusable plan template and an evidence collector. After the standalone and real Wally runs, generate `verification-evidence.json` using the commands in that chapter. Current source/artifact identities and expected checker completions are checked; equivalence, measured cross coverage, timing, physical and manufacturing obligations remain visible where unexecuted. This dossier complements the runner report rather than turning a simulation PASS into a physical qualification.

## Reproduce publication of the complete book {#sec-reproducible-publication}

The publishing environment is separate from the hardware teaching container. Work from the **full Git repository root**, not the laboratory ZIP: the ZIP intentionally omits the Quarto project configuration and publishing workflow. Docker Desktop must use Linux containers. No native Quarto, TeX installation or `rsvg-convert` installation is required on Windows.

Build the Linux/amd64 environment on Linux, WSL or PowerShell:

```bash
docker build --platform linux/amd64 -f tools/book/Dockerfile -t from-concept-book:2026.10 .
```

The Dockerfile fixes the Ubuntu base digest and Quarto to **1.10.19**, checking the downloaded Debian package's SHA-256. `tools/book/ubuntu-packages.lock` fixes all 134 additional Ubuntu packages, including dependencies, by filename, version and SHA-256. The lock was resolved from authenticated Ubuntu metadata on 14 October 2026. It includes LuaLaTeX, the required LaTeX packages, fonts, Python and `rsvg-convert`. A small fetcher image is also fixed by digest. Parallel downloads use the recorded archive URLs and verify every package before installation; archived versions can fall back to the dated Ubuntu snapshot. Building the environment does not resolve newer package versions. The initial environment build needs network access. There are no package installations during rendering; missing dependencies fail the build instead of silently selecting newer packages. The original SVG diagrams, including the executable-project diagram, require no browser download.

Render on Linux or WSL with the host user's identity:

```bash
image_id=$(docker image inspect --format '{{.Id}}' from-concept-book:2026.10)
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 --network none \
  --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" --env HOME=/tmp \
  --env BOOK_IMAGE_ID="$image_id" \
  --mount "type=bind,source=$PWD,target=/work" from-concept-book:2026.10
```

On Windows, use PowerShell and the Windows bind mount's access controls:

```powershell
$imageId = docker image inspect --format '{{.Id}}' from-concept-book:2026.10
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 --network none --env HOME=/tmp `
  --env "BOOK_IMAGE_ID=$imageId" `
  --mount "type=bind,source=$PWD,target=/work" from-concept-book:2026.10
```

The common entry point, `tools/book/build.py`, copies source inputs to an isolated temporary directory and renders all configured formats. Previously rendered HTML, LaTeX intermediates and old PDFs are excluded. It checks every chapter and appendix HTML output, the complete PDF, the laboratory ZIP and the HTML PDF download link before replacing `_book/release`. A failed render keeps the previous release. Existing files directly in `_book` are unaffected.

The results are `_book/release/index.html`, `_book/release/From-Concept-to-Silicon.pdf` and `_book/release/downloads/hardware-design-labs.zip`. The HTML sidebar exposes the PDF download. `build-manifest.json` records the Git revision, whether tracked local sources were modified, the image identity, installed package versions, tool versions, source hashes and output hashes. Local edits are useful for previews but do not constitute a validated published revision. Reproducibility here means rebuilding the recorded source with the recorded environment; identical PDF bytes are not promised, because metadata and renderer timestamps can differ. Preserve the image with `docker save` when archiving a course release.

### Publication gate and failure handling

`publish.yml` calls `labs.yml` as a reusable workflow using the same repository commit. Publication follows this dependency chain:

1. **Validate:** recipe contracts, automatic labs, negative tests, pinned Wally accelerator firmware, real Wally divider exploration and verification evidence must succeed.
2. **Build:** the offline environment produces and checks HTML, PDF and figures from that revision. Actions retains the PDF and build manifest as a downloadable artifact.
3. **Deploy:** only a successful build and validation on `main` can upload the complete release to GitHub Pages. Pull requests run validation and construction without deploying. Manual publication also requires validation; it does not bypass the gate.

Select **GitHub Actions** as the repository's Pages source. If a check fails, inspect the failed job and its laboratory evidence or render log; fix the source and rerun the workflow. Publishing an old output directory would only conceal the failure. The Docker build may take several minutes on a fresh runner because it installs the PDF toolchain. The publication gate checks the supplied executable experiments, not completion of every guided FPGA, ASIC or manufacturing exercise.

The workflow mechanism and book download settings follow the [GitHub reusable-workflow documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/reuse-automations/reuse-workflows) and [Quarto book-output documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/books/book-output.html). SVG conversion follows [Quarto's PDF guidance](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/pdf-basics).

## Optional boot and software-stack environment

The [asynchronous-FIFO practice](../labs/24-async-fifo/README.md) develops @sec-async-fifo in the ordinary lab image. It uses actual independent simulator clocks, power-of-two storage, registered Gray pointers, coordinated reset epochs and an independent queue oracle. The checked dossier includes 48 runs, six generic netlists and four detected defects. It is an explicit guided entry outside `run all`; its XDC remains a physical-integration template.

The [reusable-IP practice](../labs/23-reusable-ip/README.md) develops @sec-reusable-ip using the ordinary lab image. It generates a portable release, mounts it read-only without the book tree, and qualifies the same accelerator RTL in AXI and actual-Wally simulation environments. Two supported profiles, generated register views, negative controls and an auditable compact dossier support RA6 without a physical board. It remains an explicit guided entry outside `run all`.

The [security practice](../labs/14-security/README.md) connects @sec-hardware-security to two existing environments. The boot image runs `python3 labs/14-security/run.py pmp`; the unit-lab image runs `python labs/14-security/run.py digital`. Use the guide's Linux/WSL UID/GID or PowerShell commands. Evidence stays under `labs/build/security/`, with a separate nested DMA report, preserving ordinary unit results. Claims are architectural QEMU PMP, actual accelerator RTL, teaching debug admission/bounded SAT and synthetic cache timing; secure boot, full Wally security integration and physical qualification remain explicitly proposed work.

The same image also supports the [RVV practice](../labs/13-vector/README.md) developed in @sec-vector-processing. Run `python3 labs/13-vector/run.py` as the container command using the guide's Linux/WSL ownership options or PowerShell recipe. It builds one bare-metal integer ELF and checks VLEN 128/256/512 with QEMU, writing evidence under `labs/build/vector/`. This is an explicit optional functional check, outside `run all` and publication gating; no Linux image, Wally vector RTL or timing model is claimed.

The [boot chapter](../chapters/04-soc-architecture/boot-software-stack.qmd) and [practice guide](../labs/12-boot/README.md) provide a separate `from-concept-boot:2026.10` container. Build it from the repository or extracted-package root using `docker build --platform linux/amd64 -f labs/12-boot/Dockerfile -t from-concept-boot:2026.10 .`. Follow the guide's Linux/WSL UID/GID policy or its native PowerShell command.

This checked one-hart RV64 practice runs QEMU `virt`, explicit OpenSBI dynamic firmware and a compiled supervisor ELF offline. It records the DTB/DTS, linker map, UART log, package versions and firmware/source/output hashes under `labs/build/boot/`. It tests the supervisor handoff and selected SBI calls, then shuts down through SRST. It is optional, outside the nine automatic labs and current publication gate.

The image pins its Ubuntu base but installs available package versions; archive the image and its report to reproduce that installation. The Linux kernel/initramfs sequence has its own source version and evidence. QEMU success says nothing about a bootable Wally FPGA platform. OpenSBI, Linux and QEMU remain external projects with their own licenses; their source trees and guest images are not bundled in the practice ZIP.
